info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 4.1: Diplomatic Transcription by Hand: Building the Ground Truth.

name.text: 01 Question: Why the Manual Step Comes First

questiontext.text: Why does the course require manual diplomatic transcription before running automated HTR or vision-language models?

generalfeedback.text: Today's transcription is the measuring instrument for the rest of the term — every error rate you compute is a distance from it.

answer.text: Automated transcription fundamentally requires an authoritative human baseline against which error rates, algorithmic biases, and hallucinated readings can be measured and evaluated.

feedback.text: Correct. Without a verified reference, machine output is simply text of unknown quality that cannot be scored.

answer.text: Manual transcription is a pedagogical prerequisite intended solely to build student palaeographical skills before delegating work to automation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The reference is a structural methodological requirement for computing CER and WER, not merely a pedagogical exercise.

answer.text: Automated models cannot process raw manuscript images unless a human transcriber has first pre-tagged the vocabulary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Zero-shot VLMs and pre-trained HTR models accept images directly; human ground truth is needed for measurement and training.

answer.text: Institutional funding guidelines mandate that digital editions document a minimum number of manual transcription hours.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The requirement is methodological and computational, not an administrative mandate.

questiontext.text: Why must today's ground truth transcription be strictly diplomatic rather than normalized?

generalfeedback.text: Transcribe diplomatically, because a model trained on normalized text learns to silently modernize — and Week 6 needs the unnormalized base.

answer.text: An HTR model trained on normalized text learns to silently overwrite historical orthography with modern assumptions, producing over-normalized errors that look clean and are invisible in standard metrics.

feedback.text: Correct. Training on normalized text teaches the statistical model to modernize, destroying the evidence needed for later editorial decisions.

answer.text: Diplomatic transcription is faster and less demanding because it ignores scribal abbreviations and punctuation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Diplomatic transcription requires careful attention to all surface features, making it more detailed and demanding.

answer.text: TEI XML schemas prohibit the encoding of regularized orthography in digital editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI supports normalization via elements like , but normalization should be applied to a diplomatic base rather than silently during initial transcription.

answer.text: Normalized transcriptions cannot be rendered into HTML or transformed into critical apparatuses.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Normalized text is easy to render; the problem is that silent normalization destroys historical evidence.

name.text: 03 Question: The Ordered Hierarchy and What TEI Assumes

questiontext.text: How does TEI XML reconcile the conflict between a text's logical hierarchy and a manuscript's physical page structure?

generalfeedback.text: Physical and logical structure both exist and do not nest, so TEI records line and page boundaries as empty milestones within the logical hierarchy.

answer.text: It represents physical boundaries (pages, lines, columns) as empty milestone elements like <pb/> and <lb/> within the logical hierarchy.

feedback.text: Correct. Milestone elements mark physical points in the character stream without interfering with the proper nesting of logical elements like paragraphs or divisions.

answer.text: It splits every physical line into an independent XML document and links them via XInclude.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI maintains continuous logical elements while recording physical breaks inline using milestones.

answer.text: It strictly privileges physical page layout as the primary XML tree, forcing logical elements to be fragmented across line elements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The OHCO model nests logical content objects; physical layout is marked with milestones.

answer.text: It abandons tree-based XML validation in favor of non-hierarchical property graphs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI XML strictly enforces XML tree well-formedness and uses milestones to handle overlapping physical structures.

questiontext.text: What is the structural function of the TEI <choice> element in diplomatic transcription?

generalfeedback.text: <choice> holds alternatives rather than deciding between them, so one encoding can serve palaeographic, reading, and search views.

answer.text: It groups alternative encodings of the same textual phenomenon (such as an abbreviation and its expansion) without deciding between them, allowing different processors to generate different views.

feedback.text: Correct. <choice> preserves both the palaeographical artifact and the editorial interpretation, enabling multiple output presentations from a single data source.

answer.text: It prompts the XML parser to randomly select one child element each time the document is transformed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <choice> holds alternatives deterministically for downstream stylesheets or applications to filter based on target audience.

answer.text: It indicates that the editor is uncertain between two different words in the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Textual uncertainty is encoded with <unclear> or <app>, whereas <choice> wraps alternative representations such as <abbr>/<expan>.

answer.text: It automatically validates that an expanded abbreviation conforms to classical lexical norms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML elements do not perform lexical validation; <choice> is a container for alternative encodings.

questiontext.text: When encoding an expanded abbreviation with <choice>, what is the specific role of the <ex> element inside <expan>?

generalfeedback.text: Encode the abbreviation and its expansion separately with <ex> marking supplied letters, so the model learns what is actually on the page.

answer.text: It marks precisely those characters that were supplied by editorial inference rather than written on the parchment.

feedback.text: Correct. <ex> identifies supplied characters so stylesheets can render them in italics and models can distinguish ink from editorial addition.

answer.text: It denotes an abbreviation that has been excluded from the critical apparatus.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <ex> stands for editorial expansion, tagging the specific letters not present in the manuscript.

answer.text: It indicates that the scribal abbreviation is an external loanword from Latin or Aramaic.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <ex> represents supplied expansion characters regardless of language.

answer.text: It instructs HTR training software to ignore the word during layout segmentation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <ex> is a TEI markup element for editorial expansion, not an HTR segmentation directive.

questiontext.text: What is the crucial methodological distinction between the TEI <unclear> element and the <gap/> element?

generalfeedback.text: <unclear> proposes a reading with reduced confidence and <gap/> proposes nothing — conflating them misrepresents inference as absence or difficulty as loss.

answer.text: <unclear> wraps a proposed reading offered with reduced confidence, whereas <gap/> is an empty element recording that material is missing or wholly illegible without offering text.

feedback.text: Correct. Putting text inside <gap/> or leaving <unclear> empty misrepresents inference as absence or difficulty as loss.

answer.text: <unclear> is reserved for physical water damage, while <gap/> is used exclusively for faded ink.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Physical damage is tagged with <damage> or noted via attributes; <unclear> and <gap/> distinguish whether a reading is offered.

answer.text: <unclear> indicates text supplied from an external printed edition, while <gap/> marks scribal deletions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Supplied text is tagged with <supplied> and deletions with <del>.

answer.text: <gap/> contains the transcriber's tentative guess, while <unclear> indicates text that is completely unreadable.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This reverses their functions: <unclear> contains a tentative reading, while <gap/> is empty.

questiontext.text: Why is it essential to encode scribal corrections using <subst>, <del>, and <add> rather than simply transcribing the final corrected text?

generalfeedback.text: Scribal corrections are transmission evidence, and recording only the corrected text destroys it while leaving the reading unchanged.

answer.text: Scribal corrections provide critical transmission evidence about readers, correctors, and exemplar relationships that would be completely destroyed by recording only the final text.

feedback.text: Correct. Preserving both the deleted and added text across hands provides essential evidence for textual history and collation.

answer.text: HTR models cannot process lines where characters have been deleted or cancelled on the page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. HTR models can process the image, but encoding structure captures the palaeographical history for the digital edition.

answer.text: TEI XML requires <subst> for every line break that occurs near a marginal note.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <subst> groups an addition and a deletion that constitute a single act of correction.

answer.text: Recording only the corrected text invalidates the XML document against the TEI schema.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Plain text is schema-valid, but omitting the correction discards irreplaceable codicological and stemmatic evidence.

name.text: 08 Question: Line Breaks and Why They Matter Here

questiontext.text: Why are manuscript line breaks treated as structural elements rather than typographical accidents in this transcription pipeline?

generalfeedback.text: Line divisions are structural here — HTR trains on lines, your zones bind per line, and line breaks are codicological evidence.

answer.text: HTR models train on discrete line images, facsimile zones bind per line, and line division constitutes codicological evidence of scribal practice and exemplars.

feedback.text: Correct. Line divisions are required for pairing line images to text in HTR training and for linking TEI <lb/> milestones to image zones.

answer.text: Modern web browsers cannot display Greek text unless every line is manually broken with <lb/>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Web browsers handle text reflow automatically; line breaks are preserved for HTR, facsimile binding, and codicological evidence.

answer.text: TEI XML rules mandate that no element may contain more than ten consecutive words without a line break.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is no such length restriction in TEI XML.

answer.text: Scribes strictly avoided breaking words across lines, so any line break represents a major syntactic pause.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scribes broke words freely across line ends without hyphens.

name.text: 09 Question: Setting Up the Transcription Document

questiontext.text: Why must you verify UTF-8 encoding, schema validation, and the pre-commit NFC normalization hook before transcribing polytonic Greek?

generalfeedback.text: Verify UTF-8, live schema validation, and the NFC hook before typing — a mixed-normalization ground truth invalidates Week 5.

answer.text: Inconsistent character encoding or mixed Unicode normalization forms (NFC versus NFD) will corrupt Greek diacritics and produce grossly inflated, meaningless error rates in Week 5.

feedback.text: Correct. A mixed normalization ground truth means identical-looking characters have different byte sequences, breaking Levenshtein distance calculations.

answer.text: Git repositories automatically reject any commit that contains polytonic Greek characters unless an NFC hook is active.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git is content-agnostic and stores arbitrary byte streams; the hook ensures consistency.

answer.text: XML schemas cannot validate documents containing Greek unless they are stored in UTF-16 with canonical decomposition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI schemas work seamlessly with UTF-8 NFC-encoded text.

answer.text: Transkribus can only import files that have been validated against an external DTD rather than RelaxNG.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The issue is character normalization and well-formedness, not DTD validation.

name.text: 10 Question: Transcription Method: Working at Full Zoom

questiontext.text: What is the primary cognitive risk when transcribing a familiar historical text, and how is it mitigated?

generalfeedback.text: Type what you see rather than what you expect, and check your line position regularly — line skip silently invalidates every binding after it.

answer.text: Reading what you expect the text to say rather than what is actually written on the parchment; mitigated by working at high zoom and transcribing difficult lines backwards.

feedback.text: Correct. Expectation bias causes transcribers to overlook genuine scribal variants, which transcribing backwards word-by-word helps disrupt.

answer.text: Over-magnifying the image causes pixel interpolation artifacts that make clear letterforms appear completely illegible.

feedback.text: Incorrect. High zoom is recommended to disambiguate letterforms and diacritics.

answer.text: Transcribing line-by-line causes editors to accidentally modernize archaic vocabulary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Line-by-line transcription at full zoom enforces focus on physical ink rather than modernizing.

answer.text: Using IIIF viewers introduces non-standard colour profiles that distort ink density.

feedback.text: Incorrect. IIIF delivers faithful image tiles; the risk described is human cognitive expectation bias.

questiontext.text: Why should an editor characterize the scribe's hand and document it in transcription/HAND.md before transcribing at volume?

generalfeedback.text: Characterize the hand before transcribing at volume, and record it — you will consult it on Wednesday to judge HTR errors.

answer.text: It establishes an inventory of letterforms, ligatures, and abbreviations, enabling the editor to distinguish between model errors and scribal idiosyncrasies.

feedback.text: Correct. Documenting the palaeographical features disciplines your reading and provides the reference needed to evaluate HTR output on Wednesday.

answer.text: Transkribus requires an uploaded markdown description of the hand before it can initiate layout analysis.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transkribus does not parse markdown hand descriptions; it is for human editorial reference and error diagnosis.

answer.text: Characterizing the hand allows automated scripts to convert cursive Greek ligatures directly into unaccented Latin text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The hand document records palaeographical observations to maintain Greek diplomatic accuracy.

answer.text: It guarantees that the hand will be classified into a recognized international palaeographical registry.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The purpose is internal project rigor and diagnostic grounding.

name.text: 12 Question: Diacritics and the Polygon Problem

questiontext.text: What causes an HTR model to transcribe Greek letters accurately while systematically omitting accents and breathings?

generalfeedback.text: Layout polygons drawn too tightly cut off Greek accents entirely, so note how high this hand places diacritics — you will adjust for it tomorrow.

answer.text: The baseline polygon envelope was computed too tightly around the letter body, cutting off high-placed diacritics from the line image seen by the recognizer.

feedback.text: Correct. If breathings and accents sit above the polygon boundary, they are cropped out of the image fed into the recognition neural network.

answer.text: The CTC decoder architecture mathematically suppresses non-spacing diacritical characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CTC can recognize diacritics if they are present in the line image and training data.

answer.text: Greek polytonic Unicode characters cannot be processed by convolutional neural networks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Precomposed or combined polytonic characters are standard targets for HTR models.

answer.text: Faded ink causes the recognition model to mistake circumflexes for paragraph division markers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The systematic omission of diacritics across lines is typically caused by truncated layout polygons.

name.text: 13 Question: Scriptio Continua and Word Boundaries

questiontext.text: What is the recommended diplomatic approach when transcribing a manuscript written in scriptio continua?

generalfeedback.text: Supply word division and declare it in the header — and expect scriptio continua to make word error rate uninterpretable in Week 5.

answer.text: Insert editorial word spaces to enable downstream collation and analysis, while explicitly declaring in the TEI header that word division was supplied editorially.

feedback.text: Correct. Declaring the intervention in the header preserves transparency while ensuring the text remains usable for computational tools.

answer.text: Silently insert word spaces without recording the intervention anywhere in the metadata.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Silent intervention conceals the manuscript's physical state from readers and downstream researchers.

answer.text: Strictly avoid all whitespace in the transcription file, forcing downstream tokenizers to segment words probabilistically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. While completely faithful, an unspaced transcription is practically unusable for standard collation and indexing tools unless declared.

answer.text: Replace all Greek letters with hyphenated syllables to mark theoretical morpheme boundaries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editorial syllable hyphenation is not a diplomatic transcription standard.

name.text: 14 Question: Consistency and the Transcription Convention Document

questiontext.text: Why is editorial inconsistency in applying transcription conventions more damaging than making a suboptimal conventional choice?

generalfeedback.text: Write your conventions down and follow them — inconsistency is worse than any particular choice, for readers and for models alike.

answer.text: Inconsistent practices make it impossible for readers or machine learning models to know whether an unmarked variant reflects the manuscript or transcriber oversight.

feedback.text: Correct. An HTR model learns inconsistency and reproduces it unpredictably, and human readers cannot interpret erratic encoding.

answer.text: Inconsistent transcriptions trigger fatal validation errors in the TEI RelaxNG schema.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schemas validate XML structure and allowed tags, not internal editorial consistency of conventions like lunate sigma.

answer.text: Git merge algorithms cannot resolve branch conflicts in files that contain variable spelling conventions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git merges text lines regardless of orthographic conventions.

answer.text: Inconsistent encoding permanently locks the Transkribus credit balance allocated to the course.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Credit consumption depends on page and line counts, not editorial consistency.

questiontext.text: What is double-keying, and why is it essential for building a reliable ground truth?

generalfeedback.text: Your ground truth will contain errors, which is why Week 5 double-keys it — transcribe now so that the second pass finds few differences.

answer.text: Transcribing the same text independently twice and adjudicating differences, which localizes errors and isolates transcriber bias.

feedback.text: Correct. Agreement between independent passes indicates high accuracy, while differences pinpoint exact locations requiring adjudication.

answer.text: Transcribing a manuscript simultaneously using a physical keyboard and an on-screen virtual keyboard.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Double-keying refers to two independent transcription passes of the same text.

answer.text: Running two different OCR engines over the manuscript image and averaging their numerical confidence scores.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Double-keying is an independent human transcription verification method.

answer.text: Typing the Greek text once in Unicode and once in legacy ASCII Beta Code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Double-keying involves independent duplicate entry to eliminate single-pass human transcription errors.

name.text: 16 Question: How Much to Transcribe Today

questiontext.text: What is the recommended target for today's manual transcription session?

generalfeedback.text: One accurate folio beats three careless ones — today's conventions propagate into everything transcribed afterwards.

answer.text: One folio transcribed completely and accurately with full TEI encoding, rather than rushing through multiple folios carelessly.

feedback.text: Correct. One accurate, fully encoded folio establishes the conventions and provides a clean ground truth baseline; careless transcription teaches the model errors.

answer.text: The entire codex, using rapid plain-text skimming without diacritics or milestone tags.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unencoded, hasty transcription produces corrupt training data and invalid ground truth.

answer.text: Exactly three lines of text, leaving the remainder of the folio to be generated by automated layout tools.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A full folio is required to establish representative hand conventions and provide sufficient baseline data.

answer.text: At least 500 lines of normalized prose across three different unrelated witnesses.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The task focuses on your selected witness's specific passage, done diplomatically.

questiontext.text: Why is it important to sample training folios across the manuscript and deliberately include difficult or damaged pages rather than only clean consecutive folios?

generalfeedback.text: Sample training pages across the corpus and deliberately include difficult ones, or the model will fail precisely where you need it.

answer.text: Neural models degrade significantly when encountering unfamiliar layouts, ink variations, or glosses; diverse sampling exposes the model to the variance it will actually encounter.

feedback.text: Correct. Models trained solely on pristine pages fail on damaged or glossed pages where assistance is most needed.

answer.text: Sampling consecutive pages causes Git merge conflicts when updating the TEI facsimile element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git handles consecutive lines normally; the issue is machine learning generalization across layout topographies.

answer.text: HTR models cannot learn character transitions unless every quire in the codex is sampled in reverse chronological order.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Neural networks do not require reverse chronological ordering; they require representative variance.

answer.text: Difficult pages require fewer Transkribus compute credits to process than clean pages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Compute credits are consumed per page or line regardless of difficulty.

questiontext.text: Why should you count <lb/> elements against <zone> elements in your TEI document before committing?

generalfeedback.text: Count <lb/> against <zone> every session — a mismatch means line skip, and every binding after it is wrong.

answer.text: A count mismatch reveals a skipped or extra line, which would silently invalidate every facsimile zone binding after that point.

feedback.text: Correct. Line skips misalign all subsequent lines with their image zones, making downstream evaluation and HTR training incorrect.

answer.text: The TEI schema mandates that the number of <lb/> elements must always be exactly double the number of <zone> elements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. In a one-to-one line binding architecture, the counts should match directly.

answer.text: Counting elements is required to calculate the exact monetary cost of Transkribus credit usage.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Credit usage in Transkribus is calculated per page or processed unit on their platform, not by XML tag counts.

answer.text: A mismatch causes XML parsers to automatically delete the <teiHeader> metadata block.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML parsers do not delete content on mismatch; the error is a silent alignment failure in project bindings.

questiontext.text: Why should the manual ground truth state be explicitly tagged in Git (e.g. git tag -a gt-f42r)?

generalfeedback.text: Tag the ground truth state, because Week 5's measurements are only reproducible against the exact version that was measured.

answer.text: It creates a permanent, immutable reference point for that exact version, ensuring that Week 5's error rate calculations remain reproducible even if the text is later edited.

feedback.text: Correct. A tag preserves the specific snapshot against which machine outputs were evaluated.

answer.text: Git tags are required to unlock write permissions for remote collaborators on GitHub.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tags mark specific commits in history; they do not control repository permissions.

answer.text: Tagging a commit compresses the XML file so that it can be imported into Transkribus without credit charges.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tags are metadata pointers in Git and have no effect on file size or platform billing.

answer.text: Untagged commits are automatically purged by Git's garbage collector after 48 hours.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commits on active branches are retained; tagging provides a stable scholarly citation point.

name.text: 20 Question: What Ground Truth Quality Determines

questiontext.text: What is the consequence of training an HTR model on a ground truth transcription that has been silently normalized?

generalfeedback.text: A silently normalized ground truth produces a model that modernizes invisibly — and standard error metrics will not detect it.

answer.text: The model learns to produce modernized output, destroying historical orthography while achieving a deceptively low CER that fails to detect the loss of diplomatic fidelity.

feedback.text: Correct. Standard CER metrics treat modernized characters as normal text, concealing that the model has learned to overwrite historical evidence.

answer.text: The HTR model will crash during the first epoch of neural network backpropagation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model will train successfully, but it will learn modernizing biases.

answer.text: The resulting CER will immediately jump above 95%, causing the training run to abort.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The CER may appear deceptively low on clean text while masking the destruction of historical features.

answer.text: Silent normalization forces Transkribus to switch from a PyLaia engine to a legacy OCR engine.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The engine architecture does not change; the training data itself is corrupted.

name.text: 21 Question: Human-in-the-Loop as a Methodological Commitment

questiontext.text: Why does the course insist on transcribing by hand before using or correcting machine output?

generalfeedback.text: Correcting a machine transcription tests plausibility; transcribing independently tests correctness, and only the second gives you grounds for judgement.

answer.text: Transcribing independently forces direct engagement with the ink to determine what is correct, whereas correcting machine output merely tests plausibility and anchors human judgement.

feedback.text: Correct. Anchoring bias leads human editors to accept plausible-looking machine guesses; only an independent reading establishes true correctness.

answer.text: Machine transcriptions are legally protected by copyright and cannot be modified without prior manual verification.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is no copyright barrier; the justification is cognitive and methodological.

answer.text: Neural networks cannot run on GPU clusters unless an MD5 hash of a human-signed transcription is submitted with the job.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Computational pipelines do not require cryptographic proof of human labour.

answer.text: Reading machine output first causes irreversible eye fatigue that prevents high-zoom palaeographical analysis.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The issue is cognitive anchoring and uncritical acceptance of plausible errors.

questiontext.text: Why is it important to note how high above the baseline the scribe places diacritics before Wednesday's session?

generalfeedback.text: Bring a validated, tagged transcription and a note of this hand's diacritic height — polygon correction is Wednesday's first task.

answer.text: Wednesday begins with correcting layout analysis polygons, and knowing diacritic height determines how much vertical margin is needed to prevent accents from being truncated.

feedback.text: Correct. Accents that extend above default polygon boundaries are cropped out of line images and lost to the recognition model.

answer.text: Transkribus requires the user to input the exact diacritic height in millimeters during account registration.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transkribus does not require diacritic height at registration; it is needed for visual polygon adjustment.

answer.text: Diacritic height determines the number of LSTM recurrent layers allocated during CTC training.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Model network architecture is fixed; polygon dimensions determine image cropping.

answer.text: Breathings placed higher than 2 mm above a letter indicate that the manuscript was copied in Western Europe.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Diacritic height is a palaeographical feature of scribal hand and line spacing, not a geographical proof.

questiontext.text: What critical toolchain components must be tested on your remote machine prior to Friday's session?

generalfeedback.text: Test your full toolchain on the machine you will use Friday — push your repository, publish your manifest, install your keyboard.

answer.text: Confirming repository access, remote manifest reachability, XML validation, and local polytonic Greek keyboard layouts.

feedback.text: Correct. Missing a polytonic keyboard layout or finding an unshared localhost manifest on Friday morning derails the remote session.

answer.text: Installing an enterprise-grade database engine to cache IIIF image tiles locally.

feedback.text: Incorrect. IIIF tiles are fetched over standard HTTP; no local database is needed.

answer.text: Purchasing a commercial GPU workstation capable of training 70-billion parameter models locally.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Friday uses hosted vision-language model APIs or interfaces; no specialized local GPU is required.

answer.text: Converting all XML files into binary Microsoft Word documents for remote compatibility.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The project strictly maintains TEI XML and markdown in Git.

questiontext.text: Why should you analyze and document the patterns in your own manual transcription errors?

generalfeedback.text: Record the patterns in your own errors, because in Week 5 they tell you when to suspect yourself rather than the machine.

answer.text: In Week 5 reconciliation, knowing your personal error patterns helps you identify when the machine output is actually correct and your ground truth was mistaken.

feedback.text: Correct. Single-pass human ground truth contains errors; recognizing your own blind spots prevents you from erroneously 'correcting' a machine reading to match your mistake.

answer.text: Recording personal error patterns is required by GitHub's terms of service for academic repositories.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Documenting errors is a scholarly practice for reconciliation, not a platform requirement.

answer.text: Transkribus uses your documented error patterns to invert its CTC loss function during training.

feedback.text: Incorrect. HTR training uses paired text and image lines, not prose error logs.

answer.text: It proves that single-pass manual transcription is always 100% accurate across all scribal hands.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual transcription is known to have low but real error rates, which error logs help diagnose.

name.text: 25 Question: Why Not Simply Start with the Machine?

questiontext.text: What is the primary operational threshold where post-correcting HTR output becomes less efficient than manual transcription?

generalfeedback.text: Correcting machine output tests plausibility and anchors your judgement, which is exactly the wrong test on the hard readings.

answer.text: When the Character Error Rate (CER) exceeds approximately 15%, the cognitive load of identifying and correcting errors exceeds the time required to transcribe from scratch.

feedback.text: Correct. Above ~15% CER, post-correction is a net loss in time and effort.

answer.text: When the Word Error Rate (WER) falls below 2%, automated correction tools cease to function.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Low error rates make post-correction fast and viable.

answer.text: When a manuscript contains more than three columns of text per page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Column count affects layout analysis, not the cognitive efficiency threshold of error correction.

answer.text: When the image resolution exceeds 600 DPI, making file sizes too large to view.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Higher resolution generally improves recognition quality.

questiontext.text: In the worked TEI example, what multiple layers of evidence are preserved that a normalized edition would discard?

generalfeedback.text: The encoding records abbreviation, uncertainty, correction, and loss — all evidence that later weeks need and that a clean transcription discards.

answer.text: Scribal abbreviations with explicit supplied characters, uncertain readings qualified with confidence and lighting source, scribal corrections across hands, and measured lacunae.

feedback.text: Correct. The diplomatic encoding preserves the physical and historical evidence that later weeks draw upon for collation, apparatus, and commentary.

answer.text: The complete biographical dictionary of every scribe who worked in the scriptorium.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI encodes textual and codicological evidence on the page, not speculative biographies.

answer.text: Modern syntactic parse trees and automated English translations embedded directly in the <teiHeader>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The example demonstrates diplomatic transcription elements like <choice>, <subst>, <unclear>, and <gap/>.

answer.text: Automated vector embeddings for semantic search across classical literature.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The example focuses on foundational TEI XML structural and palaeographical markup.

questiontext.text: Which verification step ensures that your diplomatic transcription is structurally linked to the facsimile images from Lesson 3.3?

generalfeedback.text: Finish and validate before Wednesday — tomorrow's work builds directly on this file.

answer.text: Ensuring every line has an <lb/> element with @n and @facs attributes matching the corresponding <zone> elements.

feedback.text: Correct. Matching line milestones and facsimile zones ensures the image-text binding is intact and checkable.

answer.text: Exporting the TEI document into a proprietary binary word processor file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The workflow uses open XML standards and web-ready IIIF manifests.

answer.text: Removing all polytonic accents so the file can be processed as pure ASCII.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The pipeline strictly requires polytonic Greek normalized to NFC.

answer.text: Deleting the <facsimile> section to reduce XML file size before committing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The facsimile element holds the coordinate zones required for verification.

questiontext.text: Across Topic 4 and Week 5, what four distinct roles does today's manual transcription file fulfill?

generalfeedback.text: Today's file serves as training data, comparison reference, verification object, and measurement reference — four roles, one artefact.

answer.text: It serves as today's product, Wednesday's HTR training data, Friday's comparison baseline, and Week 5's reference for scoring machine CER and WER.

feedback.text: Correct. A single carefully transcribed artifact anchors every subsequent computational stage and evaluation metric.

answer.text: A draft syllabus, a grading rubric, a student roster, and a final course transcript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Today's file is a scholarly digital transcription serving specific pipeline roles.

answer.text: An OCR engine configuration script, an image compression profile, a CSS stylesheet, and a web server config.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are system administration tasks unrelated to the transcribed TEI file.

answer.text: A replacement for the original codex, a legal copyright declaration, a grant application, and a print publisher contract.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The file is a scholarly encoding serving training, reference, and measurement roles.

name.text: 29 Question: What Counts as Good Work Here

questiontext.text: Why is marking a difficult reading as <unclear> considered a hallmark of good scholarly transcription rather than an editorial failure?

generalfeedback.text: Marking uncertainty honestly is the hardest and most diagnostic part of good transcription — a confident guess destroys the record of what was actually legible.

answer.text: It honestly records the limits of decipherment from the ink, preserving evidence of ambiguity rather than presenting a confident guess as an established fact.

feedback.text: Correct. A confident guess destroys the record of what was actually legible, misleading subsequent readers and distorting error rates.

answer.text: Marking readings as <unclear> automatically triggers Transkribus to allocate extra compute credits.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transkribus does not alter credit billing based on XML uncertainty tags.

answer.text: The TEI schema rejects any transcription that does not mark at least 15% of its words as <unclear>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI schemas have no minimum requirement for uncertainty elements.

answer.text: It indicates that the editor has delegated the transcription of that word to an external commercial service.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <unclear> is a scholarly qualification of reduced confidence by the transcriber.

questiontext.text: Why is the manual diplomatic transcription step considered irreducible in computational philology?

generalfeedback.text: Automation is always measured against a reference, and a reference cannot be produced by the thing it measures — which is why the manual step is irreducible rather than merely traditional.

answer.text: A measuring instrument cannot calibrate itself; automated models cannot evaluate their own accuracy, so an independent human ground truth is structurally necessary as a baseline.

feedback.text: Correct. Machine output is just text of unquantified quality until measured against an independently produced reference.

answer.text: Manual transcription is required because neural networks are incapable of learning non-Latin alphabets.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Neural models learn non-Latin scripts effectively given adequate training data.

answer.text: International copyright laws forbid computers from processing historical manuscripts without prior human transcription.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is no such legal prohibition.

answer.text: Computing CER requires proprietary hardware that only human transcribers can operate.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CER is a mathematical calculation (Levenshtein distance) requiring a reference text.
